title: Glossary: Databricks, Microsoft Copilot, Microsoft Fabric and other agent platforms

format.aliases: Words that count as a mention of the term in a question. Matching ignores case and allows a plural 's', except for all-capital acronyms and aliases that start with '=', which must match exactly.
format.related: Ids of terms to read alongside this one.
format.decks: Optional. When present, the term is only matched in these decks (databricks, copilot, fabric, agents).

terms.definition: Microsoft's paid AI assistant for work: $30 per user per month (list) as an add-on to eligible Microsoft 365 plans, or included in E7. It grounds answers in each user's work data through Microsoft Graph and Work IQ and adds Copilot inside Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams. The seat covers 'everyday AI'. Long-running agentic work such as Cowork is billed separately in Copilot Credits.

The AI chat that comes at no extra cost with eligible Microsoft 365 licenses. It's grounded on the web, not on organizational data through Microsoft Graph, and is protected by Enterprise Data Protection when users sign in with Entra ID. Work content gets in only through uploads, open documents in Teams or Outlook, or pay-as-you-go agents.

The small and medium business version of Microsoft 365 Copilot for organizations with up to 300 users on Microsoft 365 Business plans. It has the same Copilot capabilities at $21 per user per month (list), on an annual commitment.

A $99 per user per month bundle (GA May 1, 2026) of Microsoft 365 E5, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Entra Suite and Agent 365. It doesn't include agent consumption such as Copilot Credits or Foundry usage, and it can be mixed with other licenses, so only some users need it.

Microsoft's enterprise suites. E5 ($60 list from July 2026) adds advanced security, compliance and analytics to E3 ($39). Both are eligible base plans for the Microsoft 365 Copilot add-on, and E5 includes some Security Copilot capacity.
Microsoft's early-access program for experimental Copilot features such as Autopilot and Copilot Code. Frontier features aren't generally available and can change.

An agentic system in Microsoft 365 Copilot that plans and runs long, multi-step tasks and returns a finished deliverable. It needs a Copilot license plus usage-based billing: model responses, tool calls and browser tasks consume Copilot Credits (Microsoft estimates about 100 to 700+ per task). Spending policies decide who can use it.
Microsoft's Copilot experience for building apps and code. It was in the Frontier program as of late 2026 and is metered in Copilot Credits. Apps it builds can run on Copilot Managed Runtime.

A persistent personal agent in the Frontier program that acts on a user's behalf, with its own Entra Agent ID and a named human manager. Its agent account carries a recurring 100 Copilot Credits per month, plus usage.

The commercial data protection terms for Copilot Chat and Microsoft 365 Copilot when users sign in with an Entra work account. Prompts and responses are covered by Microsoft's enterprise data commitments and aren't used to train foundation models.

The API and data layer over a tenant's Microsoft 365 content: mail, files, chats, calendars, sites and people. Copilot grounds its answers in Graph data, respecting each user's permissions. In Copilot Studio, grounding on it is billed as tenant graph grounding.

Microsoft 365's vector index of tenant content, which helps Copilot find relevant information. It honors each user's access, so it surfaces anything a user can technically open, overshared files included.

The Microsoft 365 context layer (people, content, meetings, activity) that grounds Copilot and agents, and that other agent platforms can reach through APIs and MCP. Work IQ API calls aren't included in the Copilot license and consume Copilot Credits.

Microsoft's umbrella for the context layers that ground agents: Work IQ (Microsoft 365), Fabric IQ (business data and ontologies), Foundry IQ (knowledge for Foundry agents) and Web IQ. It reached GA at Ignite 2026 with no new SKU.

Connectors, formerly Microsoft Graph connectors, that index external content into Microsoft 365 so Copilot and agents can ground on it. In Copilot Chat, agents grounded on connector content are metered for unlicensed users.

Microsoft's 2026 split of Copilot pricing. 'Everyday AI' (chat, Copilot in the Office apps, automatic model selection) is included in the per-user license, within limits. 'Advanced AI' (Cowork, Code, Autopilot, Work IQ APIs, some frontier models, advanced SharePoint work) is usage-based and billed in Copilot Credits.

A built-in Microsoft 365 Copilot agent for deep, multi-step research across Microsoft Graph, Copilot connectors and the web, with citations. Complex requests can take 10 to 45 minutes. It's included with the Copilot license and capped at 25 queries per user per month in Microsoft's FAQ. Its only web control is the tenant-wide web search setting.

A built-in Microsoft 365 Copilot agent that reasons like a data scientist over the data a user gives it, running Python with the code visible. Microsoft says it suits Excel-related tasks. It's included with the Copilot license. It analyzes the files a user provides rather than querying a governed semantic layer, so check where metric definitions and row-level security come from.

Microsoft 365 admin center reports (Reports > Usage > Microsoft Copilot). They show enabled and active users (an active user submitted a prompt), the active-user rate, prompts, and each user's last activity by app, over 7, 28, 90 or 180 days. The readiness tab flags the top 25% of unlicensed users by app usage as suggested candidates. A separate Copilot Chat report covers unlicensed users only. Names are hidden by default.

The Viva Insights dashboard for Copilot readiness, adoption, impact (actions, estimated assisted hours and value) and sentiment. It starts with one Copilot license. At 50+ Copilot or Viva Insights licenses it adds agent insights, benchmarks and trendlines. Data refreshes daily over 28 days with up to six days of delay. Microsoft calls it decision support, not an exact ledger.

Admin-authored prompts shown inside Windows and Teams. From the Copilot usage report, admins can target licensed users with no Copilot use in a rolling 30 days and track views and clicks: nudge first, reassign seats later.

Microsoft's low-code platform for building agents, including custom engine agents, from knowledge sources, tools (connectors, MCP), topics and agent flows. Usage is billed in Copilot Credits, except employee-facing use by Microsoft 365 Copilot licensed users in Microsoft channels. Power Platform data policies govern it.

The lightweight builder inside Microsoft 365 Copilot for creating declarative agents from instructions and knowledge. Generative answers from Agent Builder agents aren't charged unless they use tenant graph grounding.

An agent that customizes Microsoft 365 Copilot with instructions, knowledge and actions but runs on Copilot's own orchestrator and models, with no extra hosting. It inherits Microsoft 365 compliance controls but can't send proactive messages.

An agent that brings its own orchestrator and models, usually hosted in Azure at extra cost and built with Copilot Studio or the Agents Toolkit. It can message proactively and work outside Microsoft 365, but the builder owns compliance and responsible-AI controls.
The catalog in Microsoft 365 Copilot and Teams where users find and add agents published by their organization, Microsoft or partners.

The runtime a Copilot Studio agent runs on. The standard harness is the established runtime that the published billing rate table covers. The Microsoft Copilot harness and the customer conversation harness bill differently, so check which harness a rate applies to.
Microsoft's hosting layer (GA at Ignite 2026) for apps and agents built with Copilot Code, Cowork and Copilot Studio. Running apps consume Copilot Credits.

A deterministic workflow in Copilot Studio that an agent can call, billed at 13 Copilot Credits per 100 actions. Runs are free for licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot users only when triggered by 'When an agent calls the flow'. Other triggers, autonomous ones included, are billed.

An agent started by an event (a new email, a file, a schedule) rather than by a person in a chat. With no licensed user interacting, its usage consumes Copilot Credits even in a fully licensed tenant.

Copilot Studio's mode in which the model decides which tools, knowledge and topics to use for each request. Tools such as the Azure Databricks Genie tool require it, and each tool call counts as an agent action for billing.
A scripted response from a Copilot Studio topic, billed at 1 Copilot Credit for unlicensed or external use.
A model-generated response in Copilot Studio, billed at 2 Copilot Credits. It stacks with other meters, such as tenant graph grounding (10 credits) when the answer draws on Microsoft 365 data.
A Copilot Studio billing meter (5 Copilot Credits) that covers steps such as tool and connector calls, triggers, deep reasoning and topic transitions. Computer use is billed at this rate too.
Grounding an agent's answer in Microsoft 365 data through Microsoft Graph, billed at 10 Copilot Credits per use for unlicensed users. It's often the largest line in an agent's bill.

A model that works through a problem before it answers. In Copilot Studio it bills on two meters: the normal feature rate plus premium AI tools at 10 Copilot Credits per 1,000 billed tokens. Output and reasoning tokens are billed, and cache reads are free.

Agents operating apps and websites through the user interface, the way a person would. In Copilot Studio it's billed at the agent action rate and isn't covered by the Microsoft 365 Copilot inclusion. Windows 365 for Agents provides Cloud PCs for it.
Cloud PCs that agents use for computer-use tasks. It's available as a tool in Copilot Studio and is eligible for Copilot Credits.

Microsoft's Azure platform for building AI apps and agents with a broad model catalog. Foundry Agent Service runs prompt agents and hosted agents (your own code in containers) with tools such as file search, code interpreter and MCP. It's billed by model inference, tools and compute, not per agent.
A no-code Foundry agent, defined by a model, instructions and tools, that Foundry runs for you. It's billed per model call plus tool usage.

A Foundry agent that runs your own code in a container, built with frameworks such as Agent Framework, LangGraph, the OpenAI Agents SDK or the Anthropic Agent SDK. It gets a dedicated Entra identity and adds container compute cost.
Microsoft's workflow automation service. Classic Power Automate cloud flows use Power Automate licensing, not Copilot Credits, while Copilot Studio agent flows are billed in credits.

Tenant or environment rules in the Power Platform admin center that classify connectors as Business, Non-business or Blocked. They also govern Copilot Studio channels, authentication, HTTP calls and MCP tools, and they're enforced in every tenant.
The admin portal for Power Platform and Copilot Studio, covering environments, data policies, capacity allocation and the pay-as-you-go billing policies for Copilot Studio.

The Power Platform connector that Power Apps, Power Automate and Copilot Studio use to reach Databricks SQL warehouses and Genie. It uses OAuth when both sides are in the same Entra tenant and a service principal otherwise, needs a premium Power Apps license, and isn't available in government clouds.

The common consumption currency for Microsoft's agentic services: Copilot Studio agents, Cowork, Code, Autopilot, Work IQ APIs, Dynamics 365 agents and more. Each costs $0.01 pay-as-you-go, less through capacity packs or P3, and credits are pooled at the tenant level. They were called 'messages' before September 2025.

Consumption billed monthly in arrears through an Azure subscription, with no commitment. For Copilot it's set up with billing policies: in the Power Platform admin center for Copilot Studio, and in the Microsoft 365 admin center for Copilot Chat agents. Budgets on these billing policies only notify. They don't stop usage.

Prepaid Copilot Studio capacity: 25,000 Copilot Credits for $200 per pack per month, billed annually. Credits pool across the tenant and don't roll over. At 125% of capacity, agents are blocked unless pay-as-you-go is attached.

Copilot Studio's enforcement point. When a tenant reaches 125% of its prepaid capacity, agents in affected environments are blocked, conversations in progress included, unless overage is billed to pay-as-you-go or the environment has its own allocation.

A one-year, pay-upfront pool of Copilot Credit Commit Units bought in the Azure portal, with tiered discounts from 5% (300,000 credits) to 20% (300 million). Purchases are final and unused credits expire. From January 1, 2027, P3 is sold only through EA or CSP.
A one- or three-year Microsoft commitment, through MCA-E, that funds Copilot Credits along with Foundry, GitHub AI and Security Copilot usage from a single monetary commitment.
A customer's contractual commitment to spend a set amount on Azure. Eligible spend burns it down: Copilot Credits bought pay-as-you-go or through P3, Fabric capacity, and Azure Databricks.

Microsoft's main purchasing channels: the Enterprise Agreement (EA), the Microsoft Customer Agreement for enterprise (MCA-E), and Cloud Solution Provider partners (CSP). Some offers are tied to specific channels, such as P3 from 2027.

A Microsoft 365 admin center control for usage-based Copilot services. It decides who can use which metered services (it grants access, not just a budget), sets per-user and policy limits, and picks the billing method. A limited monthly budget cuts users off until the 1st, and 'Auto-apply new services' is on by default.

Microsoft's subscription rules for seat-based licenses. Seats can be reduced or cancelled for a prorated refund only within seven calendar days of purchase or renewal. After that the count can rise mid-term but only fall at renewal. Terms are one month, one year or three years, and a monthly term allows cancellation at the end of any month.
A contract term that stops a customer from reducing license counts at renewal. Gartner advised avoiding them in 2026 Microsoft AI deals, so customers can respond to price and product changes.

Microsoft's AI assistant for security operations, consumed in Security Compute Units (SCUs). Microsoft 365 E5 and E7 include 400 SCUs a month for every 1,000 paid licenses (up to 10,000), with no rollover.

Microsoft's cloud identity service, formerly Azure Active Directory. It authenticates users, groups, service principals and managed identities, and enforces Conditional Access. Copilot, Fabric and Azure Databricks all sign users in with it.

A dedicated identity type for AI agents in Entra. Agent identities are created from blueprints and support OAuth 2.0, MCP and A2A. Extending Entra security features such as Conditional Access to agents requires Agent 365. At Ignite 2026, Microsoft previewed agent identities for local agents such as GitHub Copilot CLI and Claude Code.
Entra policies that allow, block or require extra checks for sign-ins based on user, device, location and risk. Agent 365 extends it to agents.

A non-human identity in Entra for an app or automation. When an integration runs as a service principal, every user effectively gets that principal's access, so per-user data permissions such as Unity Catalog row filters can't tell users apart.

An Entra identity that Azure manages for a resource, such as a Foundry project or a Databricks Access Connector, so no secrets need storing. Like a service principal, it represents the workload, not the end user.

An OAuth flow in which a service calls a downstream API with the signed-in user's identity rather than its own. Genie integrations and Foundry MCP tools use it to keep per-user Unity Catalog permissions in force.

Microsoft's control plane for agents (GA May 2026, $15 per user per month standalone or included in E7). It provides an agent registry in the Microsoft 365 admin center, approval workflows, ownerless-agent detection, risk signals from Defender, Entra and Purview, and Copilot Credits cost management, covering Microsoft, partner and third-party agents.
Microsoft's data security and compliance suite: sensitivity labels, DLP, audit, eDiscovery, retention, Insider Risk and DSPM for AI. It covers Copilot interactions and Fabric items.

Purview labels, such as Confidential, applied to files, emails and Fabric items, optionally with encryption. For Copilot to return encrypted content, the user needs both EXTRACT and VIEW usage rights.

Purview data loss prevention policies. For Copilot, they can stop Copilot and agents from processing items with chosen sensitivity labels, and a 2026 preview extends that to sensitive files without labels. In Fabric, DLP covers lakehouses, warehouses, databases and semantic models.
Purview's data security posture management for AI. It reports AI activity, offers ready-made policies and runs weekly oversharing assessments on the top 100 SharePoint sites, with remediation links.
A Purview solution that detects risky user behavior. Its 'Risky AI usage' template flags prompt injection attempts and access to protected material through AI.
Purview's tenant-wide activity log. It records Copilot prompts and responses, Copilot Studio maker activity and Fabric user activity for investigations and compliance.
Purview's legal search and hold tool. Copilot prompts and responses are stored in users' mailboxes and can be found with a 'Copilot activity' condition.

Content that more people can access than should, such as sites shared with 'Everyone Except External Users'. AI assistants respect permissions, so they surface overshared content quickly. The fix is at the permission layer, with temporary discovery controls such as RCD only while you clean up.
A built-in group that covers every internal user. Content shared with it is a common source of Copilot oversharing, and SharePoint Advanced Management reports highlight it.

A SharePoint site setting that hides the site's content from org-wide search and Copilot discovery without changing permissions, so users with access can still open the content directly. Microsoft calls it a temporary control, and it doesn't cover OneDrive.

A retiring control that limited org-wide search and Copilot to an allow list of up to 100 sites. It isn't a security boundary, and new enablement has been blocked since July 31, 2026, in favor of RCD.
A SharePoint Advanced Management policy that limits a site to members of specified groups, even if items were shared more widely. Unlike RCD, it's a real access boundary.

SharePoint's governance tools for content sprawl, lifecycle and oversharing: data access governance reports, site access reviews, RAC, RCD, block download and agent insights. A tenant gets them once it has at least one Microsoft 365 Copilot license.
SharePoint Advanced Management reports on sites with broad permissions, sharing links, EEEU exposure and sensitivity labels. They feed site access reviews, in which site owners fix their own sharing.
Microsoft's commitment to store and process EU customers' data within the EU for covered services, Copilot included. Anthropic models used in Copilot are currently excluded.
A control that requires customer approval before Microsoft engineers access customer content during support. It doesn't cover Copilot Studio security audit telemetry or Agent 365 governance events.

Encryption keys the customer controls in Azure Key Vault instead of Microsoft-managed keys. They're available for Copilot Studio environments and Fabric workspaces (F SKUs only), and revoking a key cuts off access to the data.

Azure networking that reaches a service over private IP addresses instead of the public internet. In Fabric, tenant-level Private Link with public access blocked disables several features, Copilot among them.

Microsoft's SaaS analytics platform. It brings data engineering (Spark), Data Factory, warehousing, databases, Real-Time Intelligence, data science, Power BI and Fabric IQ together on one lake (OneLake), paid for with capacity.

The compute pool that Fabric workloads run on, sized in capacity units (an F64 has 64 CUs). It's billed per second pay-as-you-go or reserved, and it's MACC-eligible. Storage is billed separately. For Spark, each CU gives 2 vCores.
The older Power BI capacity SKUs (P1 lines up with F64). They're being retired in favor of Fabric F SKUs and remain only for existing Enterprise Agreement customers.

A Fabric capacity with no provisioned compute, listed on Microsoft's pricing page with on-demand billing by default, so usage is billed as it's consumed. Some features, such as surge protection, need provisioned capacity.

Pay-as-you-go billing for Fabric usage outside a provisioned capacity. With on-demand Spark, jobs stop drawing on capacity CUs and are billed separately, with no bursting or fallback. Reservation discounts don't apply.
A free 60-day capacity (F4 or F64 size) for evaluation. It doesn't support Copilot, AI experiences such as data agents, Private Link or free mirroring storage, and its items go inactive when it ends.
A commitment to a number of Fabric CUs at a discount versus pay-as-you-go. The discount applies hourly to CUs only, not to storage or networking, and overage is still billed at pay-as-you-go rates.

Capacity use beyond what's provisioned. In Fabric, paid overage is on by default, priced at pay-as-you-go rates even on reserved capacity, and checked every 5 minutes, so it can pass the limit an admin sets.

How Fabric spreads the cost of an operation over time: interactive operations over 5 to 64 minutes, background operations over 24 hours. It lets small capacities run big jobs, but heavy jobs keep using headroom long after they finish.
Fabric operations temporarily using more compute than the SKU provides (Spark can burst to 3x), with smoothing paying it back over time.

What Fabric does when a capacity has used too much future capacity. After 10 minutes it delays interactive requests, after 60 minutes it rejects them, and after 24 hours it rejects every new request. Jobs already running finish.
The capacity debt that builds up when usage exceeds what smoothing can absorb. Unused CUs in later timepoints pay it down. Pausing the capacity bills it immediately and resets it.

Fabric settings that reject new background operations once a capacity, or a single workspace, passes a threshold over 24 hours, protecting interactive users from runaway jobs. Workspace limits are soft and checked every five minutes.
Microsoft's Power BI app for monitoring Fabric capacity use and throttling over 14 days, with 10 to 15 minutes of delay. It can't alert, so use Real-Time hub capacity events for alerts.
A Fabric capacity set aside to absorb Copilot and data agent usage for chosen users, instead of billing the capacity that holds the content. The minimum is F2 or P1.

AI assistance inside Fabric and Power BI experiences: notebooks, Data Factory, warehouse, SQL, Real-Time Intelligence and reports. It runs on Fabric capacity (F2+ or P1+) rather than per-user licenses and isn't available on trial capacities.

A full-screen Power BI chat (preview) that finds and answers questions across reports and semantic models a user can access. It needs F2+ or P1+ capacity, and Pro or PPU alone isn't enough. When a question isn't about the model's data, it answers from general model knowledge. Microsoft has announced it's retiring, while Copilot within reports continues.
OpenAI models hosted in Azure, which Copilot in Fabric uses. They're hosted in US and EU regions, so other geographies need cross-geo processing turned on.

A tenant setting that lets AI requests be processed outside the capacity's or workspace's geography. Fabric AI features such as Copilot and data agents need it in many regions, and Databricks has a similar setting, so turning it on is a data residency decision.

Fabric's single, tenant-wide data lake, built on ADLS, with tables stored as Delta Parquet (Iceberg is also supported). Every workspace is a container in it. Storage is billed per GB, and reads and writes consume capacity CUs.

A pointer that makes data stored elsewhere (another Fabric item, ADLS, S3, GCS, Dataverse and more) appear in OneLake without copying it. Internal shortcuts use the caller's identity, and external ones use a cloud connection's credentials. Reads are billed to the capacity of the workspace that holds the shortcut.

Grant-only data access roles in OneLake with table, row and column security, enforced across Spark, SQL endpoints, semantic models and Power BI. Workspace Admins, Members and Contributors bypass it, so it restricts only Viewers and users with item Read permission.
Fabric's central place to discover, govern and secure data, with Explore, Govern and Secure tabs plus admin settings.
Optional disaster recovery that replicates OneLake data asynchronously to the Azure-paired region. It adds separate storage charges and makes writes cost more, and a failover can lose data.

Admin, Member, Contributor and Viewer. All four can read lakehouse data through the SQL endpoint, but only Admin, Member and Contributor can read through Spark and OneLake, and they also bypass OneLake security. Read-only users should be Viewers.
A business grouping of workspaces, such as Finance, used for discovery and for delegating some governance settings. Domains don't control access.
A Fabric-managed service principal for a workspace, used for trusted access to firewall-enabled ADLS Gen2 and for connections. Deleting it is permanent and breaks the items that depend on it.
Admin switches that turn Fabric features on for everyone or for chosen groups. Changes take up to 15 minutes, and Microsoft says tenant settings aren't a security boundary.

A Fabric item that stores files and Delta tables in OneLake. Spark writes to it, and its automatic SQL analytics endpoint gives read-only T-SQL access. Databricks uses 'lakehouse' for its whole platform architecture.
Fabric's SQL data warehouse, with full T-SQL DDL and DML and multi-table transactions, storing data as Delta in OneLake. Unlike a lakehouse's SQL endpoint, it accepts writes.
The read-only T-SQL endpoint that Fabric creates for each lakehouse, mirrored database and SQL database. It picks up changes through a metadata sync that normally lags by under a minute.
An operational database built on the Azure SQL Database engine. It runs on Fabric capacity and is replicated into OneLake automatically for analytics.

Fabric's way of bringing external data into OneLake, in three forms. Database mirroring replicates data in near real time, with free replication compute and 1 TB of free storage per CU. Metadata mirroring, which Azure Databricks uses, works through shortcuts. Open mirroring lets apps push changes in. Queries against mirrored data use capacity.
Fabric mirroring in which any app or partner writes change files into a OneLake landing zone and Fabric merges them into Delta tables.

A Fabric item that mirrors a Unity Catalog catalog's metadata and reads its Delta files through shortcuts. Tables with row filters or column masks, views and metric views aren't mirrored, and access through Fabric is governed by Fabric, not Unity Catalog.

A Databricks feature that exposes Fabric lakehouses and warehouses as a foreign catalog in Unity Catalog, so Databricks compute can query OneLake data in place, read-only. It authenticates with a managed identity or service principal.

A Power BI storage mode that reads Delta tables in OneLake directly, loading columns into memory on demand instead of importing a copy. Direct Lake on SQL can fall back to DirectQuery. Direct Lake on OneLake can't, and it ignores row-level security set on the SQL endpoint. Each SKU has guardrails.
A Direct Lake refresh that only updates metadata so the model points at the latest Delta Parquet files. Queries see data as of the last framing.
A Power BI mode that sends queries to the source system live for every visual. Data is always fresh, but performance depends on the source. Direct Lake on SQL falls back to it in some cases.
A Power BI mode that copies data into the semantic model on each refresh. Queries are fast, but data is only as fresh as the last refresh, and model size limits depend on the license or capacity.
A Power BI model (formerly called a dataset) with the tables, relationships, measures and security that reports query. Fabric data agents can use semantic models, and their RLS and CLS still apply.

Microsoft's BI service, now part of Fabric. Building and sharing need Pro ($14) or Premium Per User ($24). On capacities below F64, viewers also need Pro or PPU, while at F64 and above free users can view.

terms.term: Power BI Pro and Premium Per User
terms.definition: Power BI's per-user licenses. Pro ($14) is for publishing and sharing. Premium Per User ($24) adds premium features: larger models, 48 refreshes a day and XMLA. PPU doesn't provision Fabric capacity.

The open-source distributed compute engine behind Databricks, where Photon accelerates it, and behind Fabric data engineering, with the Native Execution Engine. It's used from Python (PySpark), SQL, Scala and R.
Fabric's vectorized Spark engine (Velox through Apache Gluten). It speeds up supported operations on Parquet, Delta and CSV without code changes and falls back to standard Spark when it needs to.
Fabric's data integration workload: pipelines for orchestration, Dataflow Gen2 for low-code transformation, Copy job for simple bulk, incremental and CDC movement, and mirroring.

Fabric's streaming workload. Eventstream moves and transforms streams without code, Eventhouse stores time-based events for KQL queries, Activator triggers actions when conditions are met, and the Real-Time hub catalogs every stream in the tenant.
The query language for Eventhouse and KQL databases in Real-Time Intelligence, built for fast analysis of time-series and log data.

A Fabric item (GA) that answers natural-language questions over up to five sources: lakehouses, warehouses, KQL databases, semantic models, ontologies or Microsoft Graph. It queries read-only with the asking user's identity and caps results at 25 rows by 25 columns. It can be used from Copilot Studio, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Teams, and it runs on Fabric capacity.
Fabric's business-semantics layer: ontologies, planning, Fabric Graph, data and operations agents, and semantic models. Its integrations in Microsoft Copilot reached GA at Ignite 2026.

A model of business entities and how they relate (customer, order, product) that agents use to interpret questions. Fabric IQ uses ontologies, and Databricks' Genie Ontology is a comparable, automatically built context layer.
Apps built on Fabric with the open-source Rayfin SDK and CLI, GA at Ignite 2026, with backends such as SQL database or HorizonDB.
Microsoft's serverless PostgreSQL database. Fabric HorizonDB, in preview, pauses when idle and replicates to OneLake. Azure HorizonDB is GA.
Software or managed services that let Fabric and Power BI reach private data sources. The on-premises gateway doesn't work with tenant-level Private Link, but the VNet data gateway does.

Databricks' data and AI platform delivered as a first-party Azure service. It provides the lakehouse (Delta Lake and Unity Catalog), Spark and SQL compute, Lakeflow ingestion and orchestration, and AI/BI with Genie. It's billed in DBUs, and the spend is MACC-eligible.
The normalized unit of compute that Databricks bills by. The rate per DBU depends on the workload type and tier.

Databricks' unified governance layer for data and AI. It provides a three-level namespace (catalog.schema.object), access control with GRANT, row filters, column masks and ABAC policies, plus lineage and audit for tables, volumes, models and functions. Its policies apply wherever data is queried through Databricks.

Unity Catalog functions attached to tables that filter rows or mask column values depending on who's querying. Every Databricks query enforces them, but tables that use them aren't mirrored into Fabric.
Unity Catalog policies that apply row filters and column masks based on governed tags, across many tables at once, instead of attaching them table by table.
Views that use functions such as is_account_group_member() to filter rows or mask columns for each user. They're the older pattern that row filters, column masks and ABAC improve on.

Unity Catalog objects that define governed business metrics and dimensions once, for reuse by Genie, dashboards and SQL. They don't mirror to Fabric, and Power BI's connection to them was in private preview in late 2026.

An open table format that adds ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel and history on top of Parquet files. It's the default table format in both Databricks and Fabric, which is why the two engines can share one copy of the data.
An open columnar file format. Delta and Iceberg tables store their data in Parquet files.
An open table format similar to Delta Lake. OneLake supports Iceberg through metadata virtualization, and Unity Catalog can serve tables to Iceberg clients.
A flexible Delta Lake data layout that clusters data by chosen keys and lets you change them without rewriting the whole table. For most new tables it replaces partitioning plus Z-ordering.
A Databricks service that automatically runs OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and statistics collection on Unity Catalog managed tables.
Unity Catalog manages both the metadata and the storage lifecycle of a managed table. An external table points at a storage path you manage, and dropping it leaves the files in place.

Databricks' incremental file ingestion from cloud storage. It tracks which files it has processed, handles schema inference and evolution, and runs as a stream, often with trigger(availableNow=True) for batch-style runs.
A SQL command that idempotently loads new files from cloud storage into a Delta table and skips files it has already loaded. It suits simpler, smaller-scale ingestion than Auto Loader.
Databricks' ingestion connectors: managed connectors for enterprise SaaS apps and databases such as Salesforce, Workday and SQL Server, and standard connectors for cloud storage and message buses.
Databricks' framework, formerly Delta Live Tables, for declaring streaming tables, materialized views and data quality expectations. Databricks manages the orchestration, retries and infrastructure.
A Delta table fed incrementally by a stream, so each record is processed once. It's typical for bronze and silver ingestion in declarative pipelines.

A view whose results are computed ahead of time and stored, then refreshed on a schedule, on demand, or when upstream data changes. It's common for gold-layer aggregates in Databricks, and Fabric lakehouses have their own version.
Data quality rules in declarative pipelines that can warn, drop invalid rows or fail the update, with results recorded in the pipeline event log.
Layering lakehouse data as bronze (raw), silver (cleaned) and gold (business-ready).
Spark's streaming engine, which processes data incrementally with exactly-once guarantees using checkpoints. Auto Loader and streaming tables are built on it.
Databricks' vectorized native query engine, which speeds up Spark SQL and DataFrame workloads. Fabric's Native Execution Engine is comparable.
Diagnostic views of a Spark application's jobs, stages, tasks and SQL plans, used to find skew, spill, shuffle and memory problems. Serverless compute provides the query profile instead.

Databricks' orchestrator, formerly Workflows, for running notebooks, SQL, pipelines and dashboards as tasks in a DAG. It supports schedules, file-arrival and table-update triggers, conditions, for-each loops, retries and repair runs.
Databricks-managed compute that starts quickly, scales automatically and is billed by usage, with no clusters to configure. It's available for notebooks, jobs, pipelines and SQL warehouses.
Clusters that run in the customer's own cloud account. All-purpose compute is for interactive work, and jobs compute is created for each automated run at a lower DBU rate.
A set of idle, ready-to-use cloud VMs that classic clusters can draw from so they start faster.
Databricks compute optimized for SQL and BI, in serverless, pro or classic types. Genie, dashboards and Power BI DirectQuery run their queries on it, billed in DBUs.

Databricks' infrastructure-as-code format, formerly Databricks Asset Bundles. A databricks.yml project defines jobs, pipelines and other resources, with variables and per-target overrides for dev, test and prod, and the Databricks CLI deploys it.
Databricks' command-line tool for validating, deploying, running and destroying bundles, and for automating workspace tasks.
Databricks workspace folders synced with a Git repository, for branches, commits, pull requests and keeping production code current.
An open protocol for sharing live Delta data across platforms and organizations without copying it. Fabric doesn't mirror Delta Sharing tables.
Unity Catalog's ability to query external systems as foreign catalogs without moving the data: databases, and OneLake through catalog federation.
A Databricks entitlement that lets business users use Genie and other consumer experiences without broader workspace rights. Data access still comes from Unity Catalog grants.
Databricks' built-in dashboards, governed by Unity Catalog and running on SQL warehouses. They're often used alongside Genie for self-service analytics.

Spark's distributed table of rows and named columns, transformed with PySpark or SQL. Transformations are lazy, and Spark plans and runs them only when an action such as write, count or display needs a result.

OPTIMIZE compacts many small files in a Delta table into fewer large ones, so reads are faster. Z-ORDER co-locates related values in the same files to improve data skipping. Liquid clustering and predictive optimization automate most of this for new tables.

A Delta Lake command that permanently deletes data files no longer referenced by the table and older than the retention threshold (7 days by default). It frees storage but limits how far back time travel can go.
Delta Lake keeps a transaction log, so you can query a table as of an earlier version or timestamp, list its changes with DESCRIBE HISTORY, and roll back with RESTORE, within the retention window.

A Delta Lake command that inserts, updates and deletes rows in a target table from a source in one atomic operation (an upsert). It's commonly used to apply change data and deduplicate in silver tables.

terms.term: Change data capture and change data feed
terms.definition: Ways to process only what changed. Change data capture (CDC) ingests inserts, updates and deletes from a source, for example with AUTO CDC (formerly APPLY CHANGES) in declarative pipelines. A Delta table's change data feed records row-level changes so downstream jobs can read them incrementally.

How ingestion handles changing data structures. Auto Loader infers a schema and can add new columns as they appear (with mergeSchema or schemaEvolutionMode), while the rescued data column catches values that don't fit, instead of failing or dropping them.
The storage location where a Structured Streaming query records its progress and state, so it can restart where it left off with exactly-once results. Each stream needs its own checkpoint.

Tools for JSON-like data: from_json parses strings into structs, explode turns array elements into rows, dot or colon syntax reaches nested fields, and the VARIANT type stores flexible JSON efficiently.

Common Spark performance problems. A shuffle redistributes data across executors for joins and aggregations. Skew means a few partitions hold far more data than others, so a handful of tasks run long. Spill happens when data doesn't fit in memory and is written to disk. The Spark UI shows all three.
A join strategy that copies a small table to every executor so the large table doesn't have to be shuffled. Spark chooses it automatically below a size threshold, or you can hint it.
Spark's runtime re-optimization, on by default in Databricks. It coalesces small shuffle partitions, switches to broadcast joins when data turns out small, and splits skewed partitions.

Failures when the driver or executors run out of memory, for example from collecting large results to the driver, heavy skew, or oversized partitions. Typical fixes are avoiding collect(), fixing skew, or choosing larger nodes.

A Unity Catalog object that governs access to non-tabular files (CSV, JSON, images, PDFs) in cloud storage, addressed as /Volumes/catalog/schema/volume/path. It's commonly used as a landing zone for ingestion.

Unity Catalog's permission model. Securables (catalog, schema, table, volume) are granted to users, groups or service principals. Querying a table needs USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on its parents plus SELECT on the table, and writes need MODIFY.

How a classic cluster isolates users. Standard access mode (formerly shared) lets many users share compute safely under Unity Catalog. Dedicated access mode (formerly single user) assigns compute to one user or group.
The Databricks UI for browsing Unity Catalog objects, viewing schemas, lineage, permissions and history, and managing grants.

What starts a Lakeflow job: a cron schedule, new files arriving in a storage location or volume, updates to source tables, or a continuous trigger that restarts the job as soon as a run ends. Time-based triggers suit fixed SLAs, and data-driven triggers avoid empty runs.

Ways to pass data through a Lakeflow job: job parameters apply to the whole run, task parameters to one task, task values let one task publish small results for downstream tasks, and dynamic value references such as {{job.run_id}} insert run context.

terms.term: Run if conditions and control flow
terms.definition: Lakeflow Jobs control flow. Run if decides when a task runs based on upstream results (the default is All succeeded), If/else condition tasks branch, For each tasks loop over inputs, and repair runs re-run only the failed tasks and their dependents.
The record of a declarative pipeline's updates, including data quality results from expectations, lineage and errors. It can be queried as a table for monitoring.

Databricks-managed tables in the system catalog for billing usage, job and pipeline runs, audit logs, lineage and more. They're the basis for cost and operations dashboards beyond what the UI retains.

Standard database connectivity protocols. Spark reads external databases over JDBC (using partitionColumn, lowerBound, upperBound and numPartitions to read in parallel), and BI tools connect to Databricks SQL over JDBC or ODBC.
Admin-defined rules that limit which compute users can create (node types, sizes, auto-termination, tags), used to control cost and standardize configuration.
Databricks Utilities for notebooks: working with files, secrets, widgets, notebook workflows and job task values (dbutils.jobs.taskValues).

Databricks' family of AI data experiences: Genie One for business users, Genie Agents for curated domain analytics, and Genie Code for developers. There's no per-seat price: each user gets a free monthly AI allowance, and compute is billed separately.

Databricks' agentic coworker for business users (GA June 2026, on web, mobile and desktop). It answers questions across governed data and connected apps, respects Unity Catalog permissions, and can be reached from Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Cowork. Usage is free through January 31, 2027, but compute is still billed.

A curated, domain-specific Genie (formerly a Genie space) that a data team builds from chosen tables, metric views, instructions and sample queries. It supports up to 50 tables, and Copilot Studio connects to Genie Agents one at a time by ID.
An automatic context layer (public preview) that maps an organization's data and business meaning for Genie One and Genie Agents, and shows users only what they're permitted to see.
The developer member of the Genie family, an AI assistant for building with code. It's billed pay-as-you-go, with a free monthly allowance.

The recommended way (public preview) to use Genie One from Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat and Cowork. Each user installs it and signs in with Entra ID. It needs a Microsoft 365 Copilot license and has no VNet support.

A Teams app that brings Genie One, or a pinned Genie Agent, into Teams chats. Each request runs as the user who asked. Copilot-licensed users can also @-mention it in Copilot. Its central service runs in East US 2 and stores only the tenant-to-workspace mapping.
Databricks-hosted MCP endpoints that let external agents use Genie Agents (/api/2.0/mcp/genie/{id}), Genie One and other Databricks services. The Copilot Studio Genie tool depends on them.
An open protocol for connecting AI agents to tools and data. Copilot Studio, Foundry, Work IQ and Databricks all support it, and it's how Genie plugs into Microsoft's agents.
An open protocol that lets agents discover and delegate to other agents across platforms. Foundry supports A2A v1.0, which is GA.

Microsoft's adoption guidance. For agents, it asks whether a task needs an agent at all, prefers existing SaaS agents, and only then builds with Copilot Studio (SaaS), Foundry (PaaS) or infrastructure (IaaS), choosing the least operational responsibility. It also covers use-case prioritization, ROI, acceptance thresholds and cost per successful task.

Copilot Studio's multi-agent options. A child agent is a lightweight sub-agent inside one agent. A connected agent is a separate agent with its own settings and ALM, which can also be a Foundry, Fabric data, A2A or Agents SDK agent (several in preview). Microsoft suggests splitting when tool choice degrades beyond roughly 30 to 40 options. Every hop adds latency.

Repeatable, scored testing of an agent against test sets of questions or conversations with expected answers, with safety evaluators and API automation for CI/CD. Copilot Studio runs evaluations as the signed-in user and doesn't support 'Authenticate manually' agents. CAF expects defined acceptance thresholds for every production agent.

How Copilot Studio agents move from development through test to production. Agents must live in a custom solution, deployed by export and import or by Power Platform pipelines. In a managed solution downstream, the agent is read-only and can't be deleted there.

A Power Platform governance feature that sends makers to their own managed developer environments instead of the shared default environment, with sharing limited to five people. Unmanaged developer environments are suspended from December 15, 2026.

A suite of premium Power Platform governance features: sharing limits, usage insights, data policies, pipelines, Solution Checker, IP firewall, customer-managed keys and Lockbox. It's included with standalone Power Apps, Power Automate, Copilot Studio and Dynamics 365 licenses.

What a Copilot Studio agent answers from: SharePoint (up to 25 URLs with generative orchestration), public websites, Dataverse, Copilot connectors and uploaded files. SharePoint, Dataverse and connectors are permission-trimmed to the user. Uploaded files sit in Dataverse and aren't. With 'Allow ungrounded responses' off, answers without a source are blocked.

Databricks' agent developer platform: Agent Runtime, durable execution, Databricks Sandbox, Lakebase-backed memory, MCP tools, AI Search, MLflow Tracing and Unity Gateway. New code-based agents are built and deployed with the Agent Bricks CLI. The earlier low-code types (Knowledge Assistant, Supervisor Agent, Information Extraction) are now labeled legacy.

Where code-based Databricks agents run, on Databricks Apps compute. The Agent Bricks CLI serves agents with DurableAgentServer, which adds persistent run state, crash recovery, idempotent invocations and ordered sessions. The older MLflow AgentServer and Model Serving's agents.deploy() are legacy paths.

An Agent Bricks agent that answers questions over documents with citations, from files in a Unity Catalog volume, a table with a content column or an AI Search index (up to 10 sources). Experts improve it with natural-language guidelines. Learn now labels it legacy and points new document agents to Genie Agents.

An Agent Bricks agent that coordinates up to 50 subagents and tools (Genie Agents, serving endpoints, UC functions, AI Search, MCP servers, other agents). Each user reaches only the subagents and data they can access. Learn labels it legacy.

A legacy Agent Bricks agent (Beta) that turns unstructured documents into structured tables, with 'Optimize for Scale' or 'Optimize for Complexity' model options. The GA path is now the ai_extract SQL function.

The MLflow interface Databricks recommends for wrapping agent code from any framework (LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK and others). It supports streaming and tool calls and is compatible with the OpenAI Responses schema.

The open-source platform Databricks manages for tracing, evaluating and monitoring agents. Tracing records each model call, tool call and retrieval with latency, tokens and cost; traces can be stored and governed in Unity Catalog.

Checks that grade agent traces: prebuilt LLM judges (such as Correctness, Completeness and Fluency) and custom code-based checks. The same scorers run on evaluation datasets during development and on live traffic in production monitoring (beta).

Ways for business experts to give feedback on an agent. The Review App lets stakeholders chat with an agent and rate answers; labeling sessions let them label existing traces. The Review App doesn't support agents deployed on Databricks Apps.

Databricks' AI governance layer, built on Unity Catalog (formerly Mosaic AI Gateway). It covers Databricks-hosted and external models, MCP services, UC functions and HTTP connections, with usage tracking, inference tables, rate limits, fallbacks, budgets, guardrails and service policies.

Spend limits for pay-per-token models, AI Functions, Genie and optionally external models (not provisioned throughput). Shared and per-user daily or monthly thresholds can email, trigger a webhook or block usage. Enforcement is near real-time but approximate, so it isn't an absolute cap.
Unity Catalog Delta tables that log the requests and responses passing through governed model and agent endpoints, for audit, debugging and cost analysis. Payloads over 1 MB aren't logged.

Unity Gateway rules (Beta) that allow, deny or require approval for a request based on the user, agent, model, MCP service, tool or request content, alongside guardrails for PII, prompt injection, jailbreaks and unsafe content.

Databricks-hosted models (open-weight and proprietary, such as Llama, GPT, Claude and Gemini) served through endpoints with the databricks- prefix. Pay-per-token is the default; priority pay-per-token costs more per request; provisioned throughput reserves capacity by the hour.

A Foundation Model API mode that reserves model units, billed in DBUs per hour, for production workloads that need performance guarantees, custom or fine-tuned weights, Private Link or certain compliance needs. Unity Gateway budgets don't cover it.

Databricks' serverless service for serving foundation models, custom models and agents as REST endpoints. Custom CPU and GPU endpoints bill in DBUs per hour; scale to zero saves cost at the price of slower first responses.

Databricks endpoints that route to third-party providers (OpenAI and Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI or OpenAI-compatible APIs). Keys are stored centrally and encrypted, and Unity Gateway can apply limits, logging and guardrails.

Databricks' fully managed Postgres with autoscaling, scale to zero, branching, instant restore and Unity Catalog registration. Synced tables bring lakehouse data in for low-latency reads; it also stores agent memory and app state.

Python or Node.js apps hosted on serverless compute inside the workspace, billed per hour while running and requiring a Premium workspace. Apps act either as their own service principal (app authorization) or as the signed-in user (user authorization).

The two ways a Databricks App or agent authenticates. App authorization (formerly service principal auth) uses the app's own service principal for every user. User authorization (formerly on-behalf-of, Public Preview) acts as each signed-in user so row filters and column masks apply.

Databricks' vector and full-text search service (formerly Vector Search). Delta Sync indexes stay in sync with a source table; Direct Vector Access indexes are updated by API. Indexes are governed in Unity Catalog, but row- and column-level security isn't supported.

SQL functions that apply AI to data at scale: ai_query calls any supported model endpoint; task functions such as ai_extract, ai_classify, ai_summarize and ai_parse_document run on Databricks-managed systems. You pay for the query compute plus inference for most functions.
A SQL function that turns PDFs, images, Word and PowerPoint files into structured elements (text, tables, figures) with bounding boxes. Limits: 500 pages without a page range and 100 MB per file.

Parameterized example SQL queries and Unity Catalog SQL functions in a Genie Agent that produce verified answers. Genie can call registered functions but can't see or change their SQL; users need EXECUTE on them.

Up to 500 test questions per Genie Agent, ideally two to four phrasings each with a SQL answer. Chat mode compares results with the SQL answer; Agent mode uses an LLM judge. Genie doesn't learn from benchmarks; they only measure accuracy.

REST APIs to ask Genie questions from code (Chat mode and Agent mode) and to create and deploy Genie Agents for CI/CD. Use OAuth user-to-machine auth for user-facing apps, and add your own retries and polling.
An agent meta-harness Databricks introduced at its June 2026 summit, with a managed version on Databricks in Beta, governed through Unity Gateway.
Secure VMs where agents can run code, with downscoped access to Unity Catalog data.

OpenAI's plans for organizations. Business (formerly Team) lists Standard seats at $20 a month annually or $25 monthly and Premium at $100 or $125; Enterprise is priced by sales and adds the Compliance API and admin retention controls. Both can buy credits for more usage.

Anthropic's plans for organizations. Team (2 to 150 users) has Standard and Premium seats; Enterprise is $20 per seat per month annually with a 20-seat minimum plus usage at API rates, and adds SCIM, audit logs, the Compliance API, custom retention and US-only inference.

Google's agent platform for work, in Business, Standard, Plus, Frontline and pay-as-you-go editions. Included seat credits cover first-party Gemini models only; partner models such as Claude and usage above quota are pay-as-you-go.
AWS's building blocks for running agents (Runtime, Memory, Gateway, Identity, Policy, Observability, Evaluations and more), each metered separately with no seats or minimum fee.

AWS's agentic workspace for business users, priced per user by edition with included agent hours (for example 8 for Professional at $20) plus a $250 monthly account fee; extra agent hours cost $3 each.

Snowflake's agent platform. Cortex Analyst writes SQL over semantic views, Cortex Search retrieves unstructured data, and agents orchestrate them. Agents bill in AI Credits ($2.00 global or $2.20 regional) per million tokens, with warehouse compute for generated SQL billed separately.

Salesforce's agent platform, priced by Flex Credits ($500 per 100,000; an action is 20 credits, about $0.10), $2 per customer-facing conversation, or per-user add-ons such as $150 per user per month for unmetered employee use. Data 360 consumption is extra.
An enterprise AI platform for permission-aware search and agents across 275+ app connectors. Pricing isn't published.
